outline.description: Provides the foundational context for the case, introducing the litigants, the patents at issue, the alleged infringement, and the initial trial outcomes that led to the appellate action.
subtopics: Parties: Plaintiff Finesse Wireless LLC, Defendants AT&T Mobility LLC and Nokia of America Corporation.
Underlying patents: U.S. Patent No. 7,346,134 (the '134) and U.S. Patent No. 9,548,775 (the '775), both covering methods for mitigating intermodulation product interference.
Allegations: Finesse sued for infringement of claims 1–3 of the '134 and claims 1,4,9,16,21,29,36 of the '775 via Nokia phones’ PIM‑cancellation feature.
Trial verdict: Jury found all asserted claims valid and infringed, awarding $166,303,391 in lump‑sum damages for the remaining life of the patents.
Appellants’ motions: AT&T and Nokia moved for judgment as a matter of law (JMOL) of noninfringement and for a new trial on damages; district court denied both motions.
Jurisdiction: Case certified to the Federal Circuit under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1).

outline.chapter_title: Legal Standards Governing JMOL, Substantial Evidence, and Claim Construction
outline.description: Outlines the procedural and substantive standards applied by the appellate court, including how the Fifth Circuit reviews denials of judgment as a matter of law, the standard for substantial evidence, and the de novo claim‑construction process.
subtopics: Fifth Circuit JMOL standard: de novo review; evidence must be 'strong and overwhelming' to preclude any reasonable jury conclusion.
Substantial evidence standard for infringement: jury findings are reviewed only if the evidence could reasonably support the verdict; incorporates the ‘reasonable jury’ test.

Claim construction: de novo review under the 'clear and unambiguous' standard; incorporates intrinsic evidence (claims, specification) and may consider extrinsic evidence under the superimposition test.
Damages review: district court denial of a new trial on damages is reviewed for abuse of discretion, following the Fifth Circuit’s controlled‑abuse standard.
Interplay among claim construction, infringement analysis, and damages: damages depend on the presence of infringement, which is in turn dependent on claim construction.

outline.chapter_title: Analysis of the '134 Patent Infringement and JMOL
outline.description: Examines how the appellate court evaluated the evidence surrounding the '134 patent’s key limitation on sampling, the expert testimony, and why the district court’s denial of JMOL was reversed.
subtopics: Structure of claim 1 of the '134: over‑sampling, isolation of signals of interest and interference‑generating signals, computation of IMP estimates, cancellation, and closed‑loop adjustment.
Limitation 1[a] requires the RF ADC to sample a passband containing both signals of interest and interference‑generating signals.
Finesse’s burden: to prove the accused radios sampled both signals; relied on expert Dr. Jonathan Wells.
Dr. Wells’s testimony: mapped DL(TX) reference to signals of interest and modeled PIM path to interference‑generating signals by citing Nokia’s technical diagram.
Conflict in testimony: Dr. Wells could not clarify that x1 and x2 matched the claimed signals; his testimony was contradictory and unclear, creating a misimpression claim.
Appellants’ argument: the modeled PIM path was generated after sampling and therefore could not be an ‘interference‑generating signal’; thus limitation 1[a] was not satisfied.
Appellate reasoning: the contradictory expert testimony failed the 'strong and overwhelming' evidence test; evidence was insufficient to support infringement; thereby denial of JMOL was reversed.

outline.chapter_title: Analysis of the '775 Patent Infringement and JMOL
outline.description: Dissects the appellate analysis of the '775 patent’s claim limitations on signal identity and multiplication, the gaps in expert testimony, and why the denial of JMOL was overturned.
subtopics: Claim 1 of the '775: generates cancellation signals by digitally multiplying three signals (S1, S2, S3) across seven third‑order multiplications, relying on summing passive IMPs.
Interpretation of 'three signals': district court accepted the term as ‘separately identifiable’ but not necessarily unique signals.
Appellants’ objection: argued that S1, S2, and S3 must be unique; Finesse’s claim amendment did not surrender this scope.
Expert testimony: Dr. Wells cited a Nokia document showing three distinct multiplications; he claimed these mapped to the seven claimed multiplications.
Evidence gap: The Nokia document listed only three distinct multiplications and did not show the seven required multiplications; mapping of the three to seven was unsubstantiated.
Appellate conclusion: No substantial evidence that the accused radios performed the seven claimed multiplications; therefore, denial of JMOL for the '775 was reversed.

outline.description: Explains how the reversal of infringement findings impacts the damages award, the procedural review of damages, and the broader implications for patent litigation, especially involving complex technical evidence.
subtopics: Infringement–damages nexus: damages are awarded only where infringement is established; thus reversal of infringement findings automatically negates the damages award.
District court’s denial of JMOL on damages and denial of a new trial were vacated because the underlying infringement was reversed.
Fifth Circuit review of damages: denial is reviewed for abuse of discretion; the court found no abuse in vacating the award.
Outcome: damages award of $166,303,391 vacated; costs awarded to defendants‑appellants.
Implications: stresses the necessity of clear, unambiguous expert testimony aligned with claim limitations; warns plaintiffs that inconclusive evidence can lead to JMOL.

Take‑away: The decision reaffirms the de novo standard for claim construction, the ‘strong and overwhelming’ evidence test for JMOL, and the critical link between evidence, claim scope, and damages in PIM‑related patent disputes.
